sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: An upper level low drifting inland to the south will maintain light showers through tonight before high pressure brings drier conditions through early Saturday. Chances for precipitation increase Sunday and beyond, alongside breezy winds and chances for coastal flooding due to higher astronomical tides.

sections.title: Short term (today through Friday night)
paragraphs: Rain showers will continue across western Washington through the evening tonight as an upper level low to the south slowly shifts inland. As the low weakens, winds will calm through the afternoon and become light overnight. Wrap around moisture from the low pressure system to the south will likely be cut off by Thursday, though a few lingering showers over the southern Cascades cannot be ruled out. An upper level ridge will build into the region as the low exits, bringing in drier conditions and maintaining near normal temperatures. The weather will stay fairly benign through Friday, with periods of morning fog and low stratus and cloudy afternoons. Highs across the lowlands will peak in the upper 40s to lower 50s, with low temperatures generally in the 30s. Near-freezing temperatures early Friday morning across the southwest interior may also allow for pockets freezing fog to develop early Friday.

sections.title: Long term (Saturday through Tuesday)
paragraphs: The upper level ridge will likely keep conditions dry through at least Saturday morning before shifting eastward as the next weather system moves into the region. A cutoff low will develop offshore by late Saturday, advecting bands of moisture into western Washington into Sunday while driving breezy easterly winds through the Cascade gaps. With snow levels around 2000-2500 feet, the mountains will see a dusting of snow with light rain showers over the lowlands.

Conditions may briefly calm in between storm systems on Monday before a negatively tilted frontal system moves into the region on Tuesday. Forecast models continue to show that this system will be stronger and more organized, potentially bringing in widespread breezy winds and snow through the Cascade passes. Astronomical tides will also peak next week, bringing increased potential for coastal flooding, which may be enhanced by this incoming low pressure system.

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: A low pressure system with an associated occluded front will continue to drive showers across most southern terminals through the afternoon. Most terminals will hold on to VFR conditions through the afternoon/evening as the rain goes through. The south interior still has the best chance for brief MVFR conditions going through the evening. Visibility reductions down to 4 miles will be possible with the rain moving through. East winds will decrease down to 4-8 kt through the afternoon and evening, becoming more northeast this overnight/Thursday. VFR ceilings will likely keep fog and mist concerns to isolated valleys/low lying areas, with skies becoming mostly clear Thursday afternoon.

KSEA...VFR generally anticipated through the TAF period, with ceilings clearing late Thursday morning. East/northeast winds 5-10 kt with gusts to 20 kt will reduce to around 5 kt tonight into Thursday, increasing back to 5-10 kt from the northeast.
HPR

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: A low pressure system spinning offshore continues to bring elevated seas and winds to the coastal waters. Small craft advisories will continue for the coastal waters as the winds decrease this afternoon, with 10-14 ft seas lingering through Thursday. The small craft advisory also includes Grays Harbor Bar through Thursday. The segment for the western two thirds of the Strait of Juan de Fuca will be allowed to expire this evening. High pressure will briefly rebuild over the waters Thursday and Friday for more benign marine conditions, and seas falling to 5-8 ft. Next weekend into early next week become active again with multiple low pressure systems moving through. The windiest period will be Monday into Tuesday with widespread gale gusts likely in the coastal waters and portions of the strait. There is still a 40-50% chance of storm force gusts in the outer coastal waters late Monday. Seas will also rise back over 10 ft over the weekend, with seas approaching 12 to 17 ft by midweek.
HPR

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: A short period of mostly dry weather is expected Thursday and Friday as a ridge moves over the region. The next chance for rain comes on Saturday as another low pressure system moves through. Rainfall amounts are not expected to be impactful. Light snow will also be possible in the Cascades and down to pass level. Conditions remain active heading into next week but exact impacts are unclear though there is a 5-10% for a strong system to bring impacts during the Tuesday-Thursday timeframe.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Wednesday...Scattered showers will continue to dissipate through the evening as a surface low well offshore moves towards California. Conditions trend drier on Thursday and Friday as shortwave ridging moves over the PacNW. Heading into the weekend, another cold front is expected to impact the region, bringing light rain and light mountain snow. Heading into early next week, active weather is expected to continue with several systems moving over the region with a low chance for a strong, more impactful system during the middle of the week.

Shifting into the details of the upcoming weather pattern. Rain and snow showers taper off heading into the evening and overnight hours along with cloud cover thinning over the area. Areas of fog will be possible as temperatures drop into the 30s where the ground will be wet. The most likely places for fog development is across the lowlands along the I-5 corridor through southwest Washington, through the Portland metro, and throughout the Willamette Valley after 10 PM. IF/where fog develops, it is expected to dissipate between 9-11 AM Thursday. Cool and dry conditions expected Thursday with highs in the mid to upper 40s inland and low 50s along the coast. Thursday night into Friday will see another potential round of fog as overnight lows cool into the 30s with light winds.

The next chance for rain is expected to come on Saturday as a trough over the Gulf of Alaska digs southeast toward the PacNW. Timing and location of the cold front still show some spread among the ensembles. The most likely timing for the front to reach the coast is between 7 AM and noon and spreading inland by the afternoon. Rainfall totals are expected to be on the lighter side with chances for 48 hour totals to exceed 0.50 inches Saturday through Monday varying across the forecast area. The best chances are along the coast at 50-60%, 30-40% over the coast range and 10-30% across the interior lowlands. There is also a chance for snow in the Cascades as snow levels drop to 2000-3500 feet Saturday evening. Accumulations over 48 hours are expected to be light with a 40-60% for 2 inches at pass level, higher chances above 5000 feet. Travel conditions could become hazardous at times.

Active weather is expected to continue into next week, exactly how impactful is still unclear given model spread. Another digging trough is expected to move toward the PacNW during the Tuesday through Thursday timeframe. A majority of models have a very strong low developing offshore which would lead to lesser impacts across Oregon and Washington. A small fraction, about 5-10% of members have the low developing closer to the coast which could bring stronger, damaging winds to the forecast area. Another scenario is the main low developing well offshore but a secondary meso-low developing along the cold front which could impact the coast. With a decent amount of spread in the main low development and possibly a secondary low, the overall certainty of a major storm is low but not zero. Details should become clearer in the next few days as models continue to adjust. -19

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 18Z Thursday...Radar imagery and terminal observations as of late Wednesday morning depicts scattered rain showers across northwest Oregon and southwest Washington as a low pressure system moves through the area. This system will gradually weaken today, decreasing showers and returning predominately VFR conditions this afternoon after 21-22z Wed. Tonight, there is uncertainty whether or not terminals will see fog development. Models suggest some clearing of clouds over northern Willamette Valley terminals this evening along with calm winds, favoring fog development. An exception would be the far east Portland/Vancouver Metro (KTTD) where easterly winds would prevent fog and low clouds. For the rest of the central and southern Willamette Valley, if clouds don't clear out enough to result in fog, then IFR/MVFR CIGs are more likely (>70% chance). Guidance suggests a 15-30% chance for LIFR VIS/CIGs across most of the Willamette Valley at any given hour between 12-17z Thu. Easterly winds around 5-10 kt across most terminals through this afternoon, then light and variable overnight.

KPDX AND APPROACHES...Predominately VFR conditions through the TAF period with light scattered showers and easterly wind gusts up to 20-22 kt through 21-22z Wed. Dry conditions and winds weakening below 10 kt return afterwards. 15-25% chance for fog development overnight resulting in LIFR conditions at any given hour between 12-17z Thu. If clouds don't clear out this evening, fog development will be more difficult.        -10

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: A low pressure system moving through the waters is bringing south-southwesterly winds to the waters south of Cape Falcon and east-southeasterly winds from Cape Falcon northward. Winds have fallen below 15 kt and are expected to remain weak through the end of the week. Seas also remain around 10-14 ft at 13-14 seconds as a westerly swell persists. Small Craft Advisories remain in effect for the inner waters out to 10 NM through 10 AM Thursday, while Hazardous Seas Warnings remain in effect for the outer waters beyond 10 NM offshore through 10 PM tonight.

On Thursday, winds briefly shift northerly as high pressure re- builds. The westerly swell will also subside, bringing seas down to 7-9 ft at 12-13 seconds by Thursday afternoon. Winds turn more southerly on Friday ahead of the next system, but gusts remain below 20 kt. Seas also fall to 6-7 ft by the end of the week.

The next system arrives late Friday night into Saturday, returning breezy southerly winds and small craft wind gusts up to 30 kt. There is also a 40-70% chance for isolated gale force wind gusts up to 35 kt across the outer waters beyond 10-20 NM offshore. For the inner waters and Columbia River Bar, chances for isolated gale force wind gusts are lower around 20-30%. Seas gradually build over the weekend as another westerly swell moves in, with high confidence (>80%) for seas building again to 10 ft or greater. -10
